questions.explanation: A higher therapeutic index means a wider safety margin, so drug Y is safer; TI says nothing about potency, efficacy, or affinity.
questions.keyConcept: Higher therapeutic index means a safer drug.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Pharmacokinetic tolerance may occur due to all the following except:
options: Decreased delivery of the drug to its receptors
Decreased number of receptors for the drug
Increased elimination of the drug by enzyme inducers
questions.explanation: A decreased number of receptors is a pharmacodynamic mechanism; the others alter drug concentration, which is pharmacokinetic tolerance.
questions.keyConcept: Receptor down-regulation is pharmacodynamic, not pharmacokinetic, tolerance.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Potent drugs have:
questions.explanation: Potent drugs lie to the left with a low ED50 and typically a steep dose-response curve; potency is unrelated to Emax or LD50.
questions.keyConcept: Potent drugs have low ED50 and a steep curve.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Regarding potency and efficacy:
options: Slope of the dose-response curve gives a good idea about efficacy
Potency refers to the different concentration of two drugs needed to produce a different effect
Therapeutic index of a drug is a ratio of LD50 over ED50
The drug response is variable in an all-or-none dose-response curve
questions.explanation: Therapeutic index is indeed the ratio of LD50 to ED50.
questions.keyConcept: Therapeutic index = LD50/ED50.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is/are incorrect concerning ED50 of drugs:
options: It is the dose that produces 50% of the maximal response in the all/none curve
It is the dose that cures 50% of cases in the graded dose-response curve
It gives an idea about the potency of the drug
The lower the ED50 the more potent the drug
questions.explanation: ED50 is 50% of maximal response on the GRADED curve and the dose effective in 50% of subjects on the QUANTAL (all/none) curve; statements A and B reverse these, so both are incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: ED50: 50% max response (graded) / effective in 50% of subjects (quantal).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is/are incorrect concerning ED50 of drugs:
options: It is the dose that produces 50% of the maximal response in the all/none curve
It is the dose that cures 50% of cases in the graded dose-response curve
The lower the ED50, the more potent the drug
questions.explanation: Both A and B swap the curve definitions: 50% of maximal response refers to the graded curve and 50% of cases to the quantal curve, so both are incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: ED50 definitions for graded vs quantal curves must not be swapped.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is/are incorrect concerning ED50 of drugs:
options: It is the dose that produces 50% of the maximal response in the curve
It is the dose that cures 50% of cases in a graded dose-response curve
It gives an idea about the potency of the drug
The lower the ED50 the more potent the drug
questions.explanation: ED50 is the dose producing 50% of the maximal response in a graded curve and the dose curing 50% of cases in an all-or-none curve; pairing each definition with the wrong curve makes statements A and B incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: ED50 reflects potency and differs between graded and all-or-none curves.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is/are incorrect concerning therapeutic index of drugs:
options: It is calculated by dividing ED50 by LD50
Can be obtained from the All/None curve
It gives an idea about the safety of the drug
Can be obtained from the graded dose-response curve
questions.explanation: Therapeutic index = LD50/ED50 (not ED50/LD50) and is obtained from the quantal (all/none) curve, not the graded curve; therefore A and D are incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: TI = LD50/ED50, derived from the quantal (all/none) curve.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is/are incorrect concerning therapeutic index of drugs:
options: It is calculated by dividing ED50 by LD50
Can be obtained from the All/None curve
It gives an idea about the safety margin of the drug
Can be obtained from the graded dose-response curve
questions.explanation: Therapeutic index = LD50/ED50 (not ED50/LD50) and is obtained from the quantal (all/none) curve, not the graded curve; A and D are incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: TI = LD50/ED50 from the quantal curve.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is correct concerning ED50 of drugs:
options: It is the dose that produces 50% of the maximal response in the all/none curve
It gives an idea about the potency of the drug
It is the dose that cures 50% of cases in the graded dose-response curve
The higher the ED50, the more potent the drug
questions.explanation: ED50 reflects potency; in a graded curve it produces 50% of maximal response, in a quantal curve it affects 50% of subjects, and a lower (not higher) ED50 means greater potency.
questions.keyConcept: ED50 is an index of drug potency.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is correct regarding the therapeutic index of drugs:
options: It gives an idea about the potency of the drug
It is calculated by dividing ED50 by LD50
Can be obtained from the graded dose-response curve
Can be obtained from the all/none curve
questions.explanation: The therapeutic index (LD50/ED50) is derived from quantal (all-or-none) dose-response curves and reflects safety, not potency.
questions.keyConcept: Therapeutic index comes from quantal curves and reflects safety.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is incorrect concerning ED50 of drugs:
options: It is the dose produces 50% of the maximal response in graded dose-response curve
It is the dose that cures 50% of cases in all/none curve
ED50 is lower in steeping dose response curve
It gives an idea about the maximum effect of the drug
questions.explanation: ED50 indicates potency, not maximum effect (efficacy); D is the incorrect statement.
questions.keyConcept: ED50 reflects potency, not maximal effect.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is incorrect concerning ED50 of drugs:
options: It is the dose that produces 50% of the maximal response in the graded dose-response curve
It is the dose that cures 50% of cases in the all/none curve
ED50 is lower in a steep dose-response curve
It gives an idea about the maximum effect of the drug
questions.explanation: ED50 is a measure of potency, not of the maximum effect (Emax), so that statement is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: ED50 indicates potency, not maximal effect.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is incorrect concerning ED50 of drugs:
options: It is the dose that produces 50% of the maximal response in the all/none curve
It is the dose that cures 50% of cases in the graded dose-response curve
It gives an idea about the potency of the drug
questions.explanation: Both A and B reverse the curve definitions (50% maximal response is graded; 50% of cases is quantal), so both statements are incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Do not swap graded and quantal ED50 definitions.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is incorrect concerning the ED50 of drugs:
options: It is the dose that produces 50% of the maximal response
It is the dose that cures 50% of cases in the curve
ED50 is lower in a steeper dose-response curve
It gives an idea about the maximum effect of the drug
questions.explanation: ED50 indicates drug potency, not the maximum effect; the maximum effect is Emax.
questions.keyConcept: ED50 measures potency, not maximal effect.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following may be used to assess drug efficacy in the graded dose-response curve:
questions.explanation: Efficacy is reflected by the maximal response (Emax) on the graded dose-response curve; ED50 measures potency and slope reflects the number of receptors involved.
questions.keyConcept: Efficacy is measured by Emax on the graded curve.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The potent drugs have:
questions.explanation: Per the source key the answer is a steep (left-shifted) dose-response curve. Note: strictly, potency is defined by a low ED50 (curve shifted left); high Emax reflects efficacy, high ED50 means LOW potency, and low LD50 means high toxicity — so this item is pharmacologically imperfect.
questions.keyConcept: Potency relates to a low ED50 / left-shifted curve (item is imperfectly worded).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is a wrong statement?
options: A drug with lower LD50 is toxic than the drug with higher LD50
The therapeutic dose used should not exceed 10% of the estimated LD50
To calculate LD50, % mortality in animals plotted against log the dose
LD50 is calculated from graded dose response curve
questions.explanation: LD50 is derived from the quantal (all/none) curve of % mortality versus log dose, not the graded curve; D is the wrong statement.
questions.keyConcept: LD50 comes from the quantal curve, not the graded curve.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is a wrong statement?
options: A drug with a lower LD50 is more toxic than a drug with a higher LD50
The therapeutic dose used should not exceed 10% of the estimated LD50
To calculate LD50, % mortality in animals is plotted against log dose
LD50 is calculated from the graded dose-response curve
questions.explanation: LD50 is obtained from the quantal (all-or-none) curve, not the graded curve, so that statement is wrong.
questions.keyConcept: LD50 is derived from quantal, not graded, curves.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is always true about a more potent drug?
options: Can produce the same response of other drugs at lower doses
questions.explanation: Greater potency means the same effect is achieved at a lower dose; it does not imply greater efficacy, safety, or clinical superiority.
questions.keyConcept: Potency = same effect at a lower dose (independent of efficacy).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is always true about a more potent drug?
options: Can produce the same response as other drugs at lower doses
questions.explanation: A more potent drug produces the same effect at a lower dose compared to a less potent drug.
questions.keyConcept: Potency means achieving an effect at a lower dose.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is the definition of tachyphylaxis?
options: Reduced responsiveness on repeated intake, overcome by increasing the dose
Acute non-responsiveness to a drug, not overcome by increasing the dose
Tolerance to a related drug from the same group
Lower threshold to a normal pharmacological action
questions.explanation: Tachyphylaxis is a rapidly developing, acute tolerance that cannot be overcome by increasing the dose, often due to mediator depletion.
questions.keyConcept: Tachyphylaxis is acute, dose-irreversible tolerance.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding potency and efficacy:
options: Slope of dose response curve gives a good idea about efficacy
Potency refers to the different concentration of two drugs that are needed to produce different effect
Therapeutic index of a drug is a ratio of LD50 over ED50
The drug response is variable in All/non dose response curve
questions.explanation: Therapeutic index = LD50/ED50 (true). Slope reflects receptor number not efficacy; potency compares doses for an EQUAL effect (not different); the all/none curve is quantal (all-or-none, not variable).
questions.keyConcept: TI = LD50/ED50.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding potency and efficacy:
options: Slope of the dose-response curve gives a good idea about efficacy
Potency refers to the different concentrations of two drugs needed to produce different effects
Therapeutic index of a drug is a ratio of LD50 over ED50
The drug response is variable in the all/none dose-response curve
questions.explanation: The therapeutic index is LD50/ED50; efficacy is shown by Emax (not slope), and potency compares doses producing the same (not different) effect.
questions.keyConcept: Therapeutic index = LD50 / ED50.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: If 10 mg of Drug A produces the same response as 100 mg of Drug B, Drug A is more efficacious than Drug B
The greater the efficacy, the greater the potency of a drug
In selecting a drug, potency is usually more important than efficacy
A competitive antagonist increases the ED50
Variation in response to a drug among different individuals is most likely to occur with a drug showing a large therapeutic index
questions.explanation: A competitive antagonist shifts the curve right, increasing the ED50. Equal response at a lower dose indicates greater potency (not efficacy); efficacy and potency are independent; efficacy usually matters more clinically than potency.
questions.keyConcept: Competitive antagonism increases ED50; potency and efficacy are distinct.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 14-year-old female with asthma treated for 4 months with salbutamol no longer responds to it. Explain the likely reason.
questions.modelAnswer: Tolerance has developed on long-term systemic use due to beta2-receptor down-regulation, so the same dose of salbutamol now produces a reduced bronchodilator response.
questions.explanation: Chronic beta2-agonist use down-regulates beta2 receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Long-term salbutamol causes beta2 receptor down-regulation (tolerance).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Compare between intolerance and side effect as augmented adverse effects.
questions.modelAnswer: Intolerance is an adverse effect appearing at doses below the therapeutic dose because of a lowered threshold to a normal pharmacologic action (e.g., tinnitus after a single small dose of aspirin). A side effect occurs at the therapeutic dose and may be a primary pharmacological action (dry mouth from antihistamines) or a secondary action (oral thrush from candida overgrowth while taking antibiotics).
questions.keyConcept: Intolerance occurs below therapeutic dose; side effects occur at therapeutic dose.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Compare between overdose and toxicity as augmented adverse effects.
questions.modelAnswer: Overdose effects occur at doses slightly above the therapeutic dose (e.g., seizures with lidocaine). Toxic effects occur at very high doses (e.g., hepatotoxicity with acetaminophen).
questions.keyConcept: Overdose = slightly above therapeutic; toxicity = very high doses.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Define drug tolerance and mention its mechanisms.
questions.modelAnswer: Definition: drug tolerance is a reduced responsiveness to a drug after repeated administration, requiring higher doses to produce the same effect. Mechanisms: pharmacokinetic tolerance (decreased drug concentration at the site of action, e.g. due to enzyme induction) and pharmacodynamic tolerance (changes at the receptor or post-receptor level, e.g. decreased receptor sensitivity or down-regulation).
questions.explanation: Tolerance arises from altered drug levels or altered receptor responsiveness.
questions.keyConcept: Tolerance can be pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Define idiosyncratic drug adverse effects. Mention 2 examples.
questions.modelAnswer: Definition: idiosyncratic adverse effects are unpredictable, often dose-independent reactions occurring in a small subset of individuals due to genetic predispositions or metabolic abnormalities, and are unrelated to the drug's known pharmacology. Examples: succinylcholine apnoea (prolonged paralysis in atypical plasma cholinesterase); malignant hyperthermia (inherited reaction to certain anaesthetics and neuromuscular blockers); haemolytic anaemia in G6PD-deficient patients triggered by drugs such as primaquine or sulphonamides.
questions.explanation: Idiosyncratic reactions stem from individual genetic/metabolic traits.
questions.keyConcept: Idiosyncratic reactions are unpredictable and genetically determined.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Define idiosyncratic drug adverse effects with two examples.
questions.modelAnswer: Idiosyncratic adverse effects are genetically mediated, abnormal responses to a drug, such as the reactions seen in porphyria and favism (G6PD deficiency).
questions.keyConcept: Idiosyncrasy is a genetically determined abnormal drug response.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Discuss 2 different mechanisms of pharmacodynamic tolerance with examples.
questions.modelAnswer: Decreased sensitivity or number of receptors (down-regulation): prolonged agonist exposure decreases receptor number or responsiveness, e.g. long-term beta2-agonists such as salbutamol causing beta2 receptor down-regulation. Counter-regulatory mechanisms: the body's physiological systems adapt to oppose the drug, e.g. chronic vasodilator use prompting salt and water retention that restores blood pressure and reduces effectiveness.
questions.explanation: Pharmacodynamic tolerance reflects receptor adaptation or compensatory physiology.
questions.keyConcept: PD tolerance arises from receptor down-regulation and counter-regulation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Discuss the types of augmented adverse effects and their characters.
questions.modelAnswer: Augmented (Type A) adverse drug reactions are predictable, dose-dependent effects that exaggerate the drug's known pharmacology. They are common, often mild but can be serious, and relate to the drug's primary or secondary pharmacological actions. Example: bleeding with warfarin due to excessive anticoagulation.
questions.explanation: Type A reactions are predictable extensions of the drug's pharmacology.
questions.keyConcept: Augmented (Type A) reactions are dose-dependent and predictable.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Enumerate two causes of a bizarre adverse reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: Causes include hypersensitivity (allergy), immune-based (acquired) reactions, genetically based reactions and idiosyncrasy.
questions.keyConcept: Bizarre reactions stem from allergy, immune, genetic or idiosyncratic causes.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Enumerate two diseases that can result from continuous use of some drugs.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include hypertension, diabetes mellitus and analgesic nephropathy.
questions.keyConcept: Chronic drug use can cause hypertension, diabetes or analgesic nephropathy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: List two examples of pharmacogenetic disorders that could affect drug response.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include acetylation polymorphism, hemolytic anemia due to G6PD deficiency, porphyria, succinylcholine (scoline) apnea, malignant hyperthermia, steroid-induced raised intraocular pressure and genetic resistance to anticoagulants.
questions.keyConcept: Acetylation polymorphism and G6PD deficiency are classic pharmacogenetic disorders.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Mention two drugs used against drug allergy.
questions.modelAnswer: Epinephrine, corticosteroids and antihistaminics are used to treat drug allergy.
questions.keyConcept: Epinephrine, corticosteroids and antihistamines treat drug allergy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: State the difference between tolerance and tachyphylaxis.
questions.modelAnswer: Onset: tolerance is gradual, developing over days or weeks, while tachyphylaxis is rapid, developing acutely within minutes to hours. Overcome by increasing dose: tolerance can usually be overcome by increasing the dose, while tachyphylaxis cannot. Mechanism: tolerance commonly involves receptor down-regulation or enzyme induction, while tachyphylaxis commonly involves neurotransmitter depletion (e.g. ephedrine).
questions.explanation: Tachyphylaxis is rapid and dose-resistant; tolerance is gradual.
questions.keyConcept: Tachyphylaxis develops fast and cannot be overcome by higher doses.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Sudden withdrawal of drugs may precipitate adverse effects. Discuss this statement with 2 examples.
questions.modelAnswer: Sudden cessation of certain drugs can cause severe rebound or withdrawal phenomena because the body has adapted to chronic drug presence. Examples: beta-blockers, where abrupt withdrawal causes rebound hypertension, tachycardia or worsening angina due to beta-receptor up-regulation; clonidine, where sudden stoppage causes severe rebound hypertension and sympathetic overactivity; corticosteroids, where abrupt withdrawal causes acute adrenal insufficiency, hypotension and hypoglycaemia from HPA-axis suppression.
questions.explanation: Chronic adaptation makes abrupt withdrawal dangerous.
questions.keyConcept: Abrupt withdrawal of beta-blockers, clonidine or steroids causes rebound effects.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What are the measures against drug allergy?
questions.modelAnswer: Epinephrine, corticosteroids, and antihistaminics.
questions.explanation: These agents treat and control allergic and anaphylactic reactions.
questions.keyConcept: Drug allergy is managed with adrenaline, corticosteroids and antihistamines.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match each adverse drug reaction type to its example.
questions.explanation: Hypersensitivity is immune-mediated (penicillin anaphylaxis); idiosyncrasy is a genetically determined abnormal response (barbiturate porphyria); mutagenicity causes gene mutations; teratogenicity causes fetal malformation; iatrogenic disease is drug-induced disease.
questions.keyConcept: Categories of adverse drug reactions: hypersensitivity, idiosyncrasy, mutagenicity, teratogenicity, iatrogenic.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match each drug to its potential drug interaction.

pairs.target: Risk of pregnancy from increased metabolism of oral contraceptives
Theophylline toxicity from inhibition of its metabolism
Kernicterus in the newborn from displacement of bilirubin
Bleeding with warfarin from displacement from plasma proteins
Chelation of Ca²⁺ and Al³⁺ in antacids

questions.explanation: Rifampicin is an enzyme inducer; erythromycin a CYP inhibitor; sulfonamides displace bilirubin; aspirin displaces warfarin; tetracyclines chelate divalent/trivalent cations.
questions.keyConcept: Interaction mechanisms: enzyme induction/inhibition, protein-binding displacement, chelation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match each drug to its potential drug interaction.

pairs.target: Risk of pregnancy due to increased metabolism of oral contraceptives
Theophylline toxicity due to inhibition of its metabolism
Kernicterus in the newborn due to displacement of bilirubin from plasma proteins
Bleeding with warfarin due to displacement from plasma proteins
Chelation of Ca2+ and Al3+ in antacids

questions.explanation: Rifampicin induces metabolism (contraceptive failure); erythromycin inhibits metabolism (theophylline toxicity); sulfonamides displace bilirubin (kernicterus); aspirin displaces warfarin (bleeding); tetracyclines chelate divalent/trivalent cations.
questions.keyConcept: Mechanisms of clinically important drug interactions.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross-match each drug to the adverse effect that may follow its sudden withdrawal.
questions.explanation: Abrupt withdrawal causes: alcohol - convulsions; corticosteroids - hypoglycaemia (adrenal insufficiency); beta-blockers - rebound angina; warfarin - rebound thromboembolism; clonidine - rebound hypertension.
questions.keyConcept: Sudden drug withdrawal can cause rebound adverse effects.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match each pharmacogenetic disorder to the drug that might reveal it.

pairs.premise: Increased risk of neuropathy and hepatitis in slow acetylators

questions.explanation: Barbiturates precipitate acute porphyria; succinylcholine triggers malignant hyperthermia/apnea (pseudocholinesterase deficiency); corticosteroids raise IOP in susceptible eyes; isoniazid causes neuropathy/hepatitis in slow acetylators.
questions.keyConcept: Pharmacogenetic disorders unmasked by specific drugs.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match each pharmacogenetic disorder to the drug that might reveal it.

pairs.premise: Increased risk of neuropathy in slow acetylators

questions.explanation: Barbiturates precipitate acute porphyria; succinylcholine triggers malignant hyperthermia/apnea; corticosteroids raise IOP; isoniazid causes neuropathy in slow acetylators.
questions.keyConcept: Pharmacogenetic disorders unmasked by specific drugs.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross-match each pharmacogenetic disorder to the drug that might reveal it.

pairs.premise: Increased risk of neuropathy in slow acetylators

questions.explanation: Barbiturates precipitate porphyria; succinylcholine triggers malignant hyperthermia or apnoea; corticosteroids raise intraocular pressure; isoniazid causes neuropathy in slow acetylators.
questions.keyConcept: Pharmacogenetic disorders are unmasked by specific drugs.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match each tolerance-related term to its definition.

pairs.target: Lower threshold to a normal pharmacologic action, seen at subtherapeutic doses
Tolerance to a related drug from the same group
Reduced responsiveness on repeated intake, overcome by increasing the dose
Acute non-responsiveness, not overcome by increasing the dose

questions.explanation: Intolerance is an exaggerated response at low doses; cross-tolerance extends to related drugs; tolerance is gradual and dose-reversible; tachyphylaxis is rapid and dose-resistant.
questions.keyConcept: Distinguish intolerance, tolerance, cross-tolerance, and tachyphylaxis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match each tolerance term to its definition.

pairs.target: Lower threshold to a normal pharmacologic action seen at doses lower than therapeutic
Tolerance to a related drug from the same group
Reduced responsiveness on repeated intake; overcome by increasing the dose
Acute non-responsiveness, not overcome by increasing dose

questions.explanation: Intolerance = exaggerated response at low dose; cross tolerance = extends to related drugs; tolerance = gradual decreased response overcome by dose increase; tachyphylaxis = rapid tolerance not overcome by dose increase.
questions.keyConcept: Distinguishing intolerance, tolerance, cross tolerance, and tachyphylaxis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match each type of adverse drug reaction to its example.
questions.explanation: Hypersensitivity = immune anaphylaxis (penicillins); idiosyncrasy = genetically determined abnormal response (porphyria with barbiturates); mutagenicity = gene damage; teratogenicity = fetal malformation; iatrogenic = physician/drug-induced disease.
questions.keyConcept: Classifying adverse drug reactions by mechanism.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match the following terms with their corresponding definition.

pairs.target: Apnea due to administration of succinyl choline
Fetal abnormalities due to taking during 1st trimester of pregnancy
Anaphylactic shock due to intravenous injection of penicillins

questions.explanation: Idiosyncrasy = genetically abnormal response (succinylcholine apnea); mutagenicity = gene damage; teratogenicity = fetal malformation; iatrogenic = physician/drug-induced disease; hypersensitivity = immune anaphylaxis.
questions.keyConcept: Classifying adverse reactions by mechanism.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross-match the following to the corresponding definition.

pairs.target: Apnoea due to administration of succinylcholine
Foetal abnormalities due to taking during 1st trimester of pregnancy
Anaphylactic shock due to intravenous injection of penicillin

questions.explanation: Idiosyncrasy is a genetically determined abnormal response; mutagenicity induces genetic abnormalities; teratogenicity causes foetal malformations; iatrogenic effects result from treatment; hypersensitivity is an immune reaction.
questions.keyConcept: Adverse drug effects fall into distinct mechanistic categories.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match the following tolerance/response terms by their corresponding definition.

pairs.target: Lower threshold to a normal pharmacological action seen at doses lower than therapeutic dose
Tolerance to a related drug with similar pharmacological action
Abnormal response of the drug due to patient's genetic defect
Acute non responsiveness, not overcome by increasing the dose
Decreased responsiveness on repeated intake, overcome by increasing the dose

questions.explanation: Intolerance = exaggerated response at low dose; cross tolerance = extends to related drugs; idiosyncrasy = genetically determined abnormal response; tachyphylaxis = rapid tolerance not overcome by dose increase; tolerance = gradual decreased response overcome by dose increase.
questions.keyConcept: Intolerance, cross tolerance, idiosyncrasy, tachyphylaxis, tolerance.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match the type of interaction occurring on co-administration of the following drugs.

pairs.target: Synergism (sequential blockade, effect greater than additive)
Potentiation (inactive drug enhances the active one)

questions.explanation: Sulfonamides + trimethoprim block sequential folate synthesis steps (synergism); two sedatives give summation; β-lactamase inhibitors are not antibacterial alone but potentiate ampicillin.
questions.keyConcept: Drug-interaction types: summation, synergism, potentiation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match the type of interaction occurring on co-administration of the following drugs.
questions.explanation: Sulfonamides + trimethoprim block sequential steps (synergism); two sedatives with the same action add up (summation); a beta-lactamase inhibitor has no antibacterial action itself but enhances ampicillin (potentiation).
questions.keyConcept: Synergism vs summation vs potentiation in drug interactions.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Match the following drug categories to the most appropriate description.

pairs.target: Drugs needed for treatment of rare diseases
Drugs that meet the priority health-care needs of the population
Drugs safe in pregnancy with no risk detected in human studies
Inactive drugs transformed in the body to active metabolites

questions.explanation: Orphan drugs treat rare diseases; essential drugs meet priority needs; FDA-A drugs show no human fetal risk; FDA-X drugs are contraindicated in pregnancy; OTC drugs need no prescription; prodrugs are activated by metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: Drug classification: orphan, essential, OTC, FDA pregnancy categories, prodrugs.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Match the following drugs/categories to the most appropriate statement.

pairs.target: Drugs that meet the priority health care needs of the population
Drugs needed for treatment of rare diseases
Drugs that induce changes in the genes of children

questions.explanation: Essential drugs meet priority health needs; orphan drugs treat rare diseases; OTC drugs need no prescription; mutagenic drugs alter genes; teratogenic drugs harm the foetus.
questions.keyConcept: Drug categories are defined by their use and risk profile.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Choose the incorrect statement:
options: Side effect of the drug is dose dependent adverse effect
Pharmacogenecity is a dose independent adverse effect
Iatrogenic disease is a disease due to using drug
Intolerance is decrease response of the drug due to repeated administration
Drug allergy occurs due to prior exposure to a drug act as antigen
questions.explanation: Decreased response on repeated administration is TOLERANCE, not intolerance (which is an exaggerated response at low doses); D is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Intolerance = exaggerated low-dose response, not decreased response on repetition.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Choose the incorrect statement:
options: Prescription-only medications (POM) are only dispensed with a prescription
Over-the-counter drugs (OTC) can be dispensed without a prescription
Behind-the-counter drugs (BTC) are only dispensed with the pharmacist or the patient
Noncompliance is one of the factors that can modify the drug response
questions.explanation: Behind-the-counter drugs are dispensed under pharmacist supervision but do not necessarily require direct patient consultation, so this description is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: BTC drugs are dispensed under pharmacist supervision.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Choose the incorrect statement:
options: Side effect of the drug is a dose-dependent adverse effect
Pharmacogenicity is a dose-independent adverse effect
Iatrogenic disease is a disease due to using a drug
Intolerance is a decreased response to the drug due to repeated administration
Drug allergy occurs due to prior exposure to a drug functioning as an antigen
questions.explanation: Intolerance is an exaggerated response to a normal dose, not a decreased response from repeated administration (which is tolerance), so this is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Intolerance is an exaggerated, not reduced, response.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross-match each drug to the adverse effect that may follow its sudden withdrawal - Alcohol:
questions.explanation: Abrupt alcohol withdrawal causes a hyperexcitable state with anxiety, tremor and seizures.
questions.keyConcept: Alcohol withdrawal causes anxiety and convulsions.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross-match each drug to the adverse effect that may follow its sudden withdrawal - Beta-blockers:
questions.explanation: Abrupt beta-blocker withdrawal causes rebound receptor up-regulation, precipitating angina (and possibly infarction).
questions.keyConcept: Beta-blocker withdrawal precipitates rebound angina.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross-match each drug to the adverse effect that may follow its sudden withdrawal - Clonidine:
questions.explanation: Sudden clonidine withdrawal causes rebound hypertension from a surge in sympathetic outflow.
questions.keyConcept: Clonidine withdrawal causes rebound hypertension.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross-match each drug to the adverse effect that may follow its sudden withdrawal - Corticosteroids:
questions.explanation: Sudden corticosteroid withdrawal causes acute adrenal insufficiency, which can present with hypoglycemia.
questions.keyConcept: Steroid withdrawal causes adrenal insufficiency (hypoglycemia).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross-match each drug to the adverse effect that may follow its sudden withdrawal - Warfarin:
questions.explanation: Stopping warfarin abruptly leaves a transient hypercoagulable state, increasing thromboembolism risk.
questions.keyConcept: Warfarin withdrawal risks rebound thromboembolism.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross-match each pharmacogenetic disorder to the drug that might reveal it - Increased risk of neuropathy in slow acetylators:
questions.explanation: Slow acetylators metabolise isoniazid slowly, leading to accumulation and peripheral neuropathy.
questions.keyConcept: Isoniazid causes neuropathy in slow acetylators.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross-match each pharmacogenetic disorder to the drug that might reveal it - Malignant hyperthermia or apnea:
questions.explanation: Succinylcholine can trigger malignant hyperthermia and, in pseudocholinesterase deficiency, prolonged apnea.
questions.keyConcept: Succinylcholine reveals malignant hyperthermia / apnea.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross-match each pharmacogenetic disorder to the drug that might reveal it - Precipitation of porphyria:
questions.explanation: Barbiturates induce hepatic ALA synthase and can precipitate acute porphyria.
questions.keyConcept: Barbiturates can precipitate acute porphyria.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross-match each pharmacogenetic disorder to the drug that might reveal it - Raised intraocular pressure:
questions.explanation: Corticosteroids can raise intraocular pressure in genetically susceptible (steroid-responder) individuals.
questions.keyConcept: Corticosteroids can raise intraocular pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Oral thrush that may occur with prolonged use of broad spectrum antibacterial drugs is:
questions.explanation: Oral thrush from broad-spectrum antibiotics is a superinfection — an indirect (secondary) pharmacological side effect resulting from suppression of normal flora.
questions.keyConcept: Antibiotic superinfection is a secondary (2nd) pharmacological effect.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Oral thrush that may occur with prolonged use of broad-spectrum antibacterial drugs is:
questions.explanation: Superinfection (oral thrush) results indirectly from killing normal flora, a secondary pharmacological side effect rather than a direct action of the drug.
questions.keyConcept: Superinfection is a secondary pharmacological side effect.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Pharmacokinetic tolerance may occur due to all the following except:
options: Decrease delivery of the drug to its receptors
Decrease number of receptors of the drugs
Increase elimination of the drug by enzyme inducers
questions.explanation: A change in receptor number is a pharmacodynamic mechanism; reduced absorption/delivery and increased elimination are pharmacokinetic causes of tolerance.
questions.keyConcept: Receptor-number change is pharmacodynamic, not pharmacokinetic, tolerance.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Pharmacokinetic tolerance may occur due to all the following EXCEPT:
options: Decrease in delivery of the drug to its receptors
Decrease in the number of receptors of the drug
Increased elimination of the drug by enzyme inducers
questions.explanation: A decrease in receptor number is pharmacodynamic, not pharmacokinetic, tolerance, so this is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Receptor down-regulation is pharmacodynamic tolerance.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Teratogenicity means:
options: Apnea due to administration of succinylcholine
Anaphylactic shock due to intravenous injection of penicillin
Induction of fetal abnormalities due to taking a drug during the first trimester of pregnancy
questions.explanation: Teratogenicity refers to the induction of fetal abnormalities, classically when a drug is taken during the first trimester.
questions.keyConcept: Teratogenicity = first-trimester drug-induced fetal malformation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following are possible causes of pharmacodynamic tolerance except:
options: Change in the sensitivity of receptors
Change in the number of receptors
Change in the delivery of drug to site of action
Change in the level of neurotransmitters
questions.explanation: Altered delivery of drug to its site is a pharmacokinetic mechanism; receptor sensitivity/number and neurotransmitter level changes are pharmacodynamic.
questions.keyConcept: Drug delivery changes cause pharmacokinetic (not pharmacodynamic) tolerance.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following are possible causes of pharmacodynamic tolerance EXCEPT:
options: Change in the sensitivity of receptors
Change in the number of receptors
Change in the delivery of the drug to its site of access
Change in the level of neurotransmitter actions
questions.explanation: Changes in drug delivery to the site of action are pharmacokinetic, not pharmacodynamic, so this is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Pharmacodynamic tolerance is receptor-level, not delivery-level.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is the definition of tachyphylaxis?
options: Lower threshold to a normal pharmacologic action
Tolerance to a related drug from the same group
Reduced responsiveness on repeated intake, overcome by increasing the dose
Acute non-responsiveness to a drug, not overcome by increasing the dose
questions.explanation: Tachyphylaxis is an acute, rapidly developing unresponsiveness that cannot be overcome by increasing the dose.
questions.keyConcept: Tachyphylaxis is acute tolerance unresponsive to dose increases.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following means teratogenicity?
options: Immune-based adverse reactions occurring with second exposure to the drug
questions.explanation: Teratogenicity is the capacity of a drug to induce fetal malformations, especially during organogenesis in the first trimester.
questions.keyConcept: Teratogenicity = drug-induced fetal abnormalities.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Alpha methyldopa: mechanism of action and therapeutic use.
questions.modelAnswer: Mechanism: a prodrug metabolised to alpha-methyl noradrenaline, which acts as a false neurotransmitter and stimulates central alpha2 adrenoceptors, reducing sympathetic outflow from the brainstem and lowering peripheral vascular resistance and heart rate. Therapeutic use: hypertension, particularly first-line for hypertension in pregnancy.
questions.explanation: Central alpha2 stimulation reduces sympathetic drive.
questions.keyConcept: Methyldopa is a central alpha2 agonist used in pregnancy hypertension.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Beta blockers are used as prophylaxis in esophageal varices. Explain.
questions.modelAnswer: Non-selective beta blockers reduce portal blood flow by causing splanchnic vasoconstriction (through beta-2 blockade) and by reducing cardiac output (through beta-1 blockade).
questions.keyConcept: Non-selective beta blockers lower portal pressure via splanchnic vasoconstriction and reduced cardiac output.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Carvedilol is used in chronic heart failure. Explain.
questions.modelAnswer: Carvedilol has oxygen free-radical antioxidant activity and reduces apoptosis, which is beneficial in chronic heart failure.
questions.keyConcept: Carvedilol is antioxidant and anti-apoptotic, benefiting heart failure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Clonidine: mention its mechanism of action.
questions.modelAnswer: Clonidine stimulates postsynaptic alpha-2 receptors in the nucleus tractus solitarius and imidazoline receptors in the rostral ventrolateral medulla, decreasing central sympathetic outflow and lowering blood pressure. It also acts on peripheral presynaptic alpha-2 receptors on adrenergic neurons to reduce norepinephrine release, and stimulates postsynaptic alpha-2 receptors to decrease renin and aldosterone.
questions.keyConcept: Clonidine is a central alpha-2/imidazoline agonist that lowers sympathetic outflow and renin.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Clonidine: mention the mechanism of action and three therapeutic uses.
questions.modelAnswer: Mechanism: a centrally acting alpha2 adrenoceptor agonist that stimulates brainstem alpha2 receptors, decreasing sympathetic outflow and reducing heart rate, cardiac output and peripheral vascular resistance. Uses: hypertension (especially resistant); menopausal hot flushes; opioid withdrawal symptoms; migraine prophylaxis; ADHD.
questions.explanation: Central alpha2 agonism lowers sympathetic tone.
questions.keyConcept: Clonidine is a central alpha2 agonist with several uses.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Compare between lipophilic and hydrophilic beta blockers in terms of absorption, first-pass effect and bioavailability.
questions.modelAnswer: Lipophilic beta blockers (propranolol, metoprolol, carvedilol) are well absorbed, undergo extensive first-pass metabolism and therefore have lower bioavailability. Hydrophilic beta blockers (atenolol, nadolol) are irregularly absorbed, undergo less first-pass metabolism and have higher bioavailability.
questions.keyConcept: Lipophilic BBs: well absorbed, high first-pass, low bioavailability; hydrophilic BBs: the reverse.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Compare between lipophilic and hydrophilic beta blockers in terms of distribution, elimination and half-life.
questions.modelAnswer: Lipophilic beta blockers penetrate the CNS more (more CNS side effects), are eliminated mainly by the liver (suitable in renal impairment) and have a short half-life requiring frequent administration (except esmolol). Hydrophilic beta blockers penetrate the CNS less (fewer CNS side effects), are eliminated mainly by the kidney (suitable in hepatic impairment) and have a long half-life allowing once-daily administration.
questions.keyConcept: Lipophilic BBs are CNS-penetrant and hepatically cleared; hydrophilic BBs are renally cleared and longer acting.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Complete: the main use of alpha blockers, and the uses of prazosin and tamsulosin.
questions.modelAnswer: The main use of alpha blockers is benign prostatic hyperplasia. Prazosin is used in benign prostatic hyperplasia with essential hypertension, while tamsulosin is used in benign prostatic hyperplasia without essential hypertension.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha blockers treat BPH; prazosin suits coexisting hypertension, tamsulosin does not.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Enumerate four adverse effects of alpha adrenoceptor blockers.
questions.modelAnswer: Postural hypotension (especially first-dose syncope); reflex tachycardia; nasal stuffiness; fluid retention with chronic use; impaired ejaculation/sexual dysfunction; headache and dizziness.
questions.explanation: Loss of alpha1-mediated vasoconstriction causes these effects.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha-blockers cause postural hypotension and reflex tachycardia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Enumerate four therapeutic uses of beta blockers secondary to beta-2 blockade or local action.
questions.modelAnswer: These uses include open-angle glaucoma (timolol and betaxolol), prophylaxis in esophageal varices, prophylaxis of migraine (propranolol and timolol) and essential tremor.
questions.keyConcept: Non-cardiac beta-blocker uses: glaucoma, varices, migraine prophylaxis and essential tremor.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Enumerate four therapeutic uses of beta blockers secondary to blocking beta2.
questions.modelAnswer: Oesophageal varices (reduce portal pressure via splanchnic vasoconstriction); tremors (essential or anxiety-induced); migraine prophylaxis; anxiety (reduce peripheral symptoms); glaucoma (reduce aqueous humour production).
questions.explanation: These uses depend on beta2 blockade outside the heart.
questions.keyConcept: Beta2 blockade gives non-cardiac therapeutic benefits.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Enumerate the adverse effects of beta blockers due to blocking beta2 receptors.
questions.modelAnswer: Bronchospasm (contraindicated in asthma/COPD); prolongation of insulin-induced hypoglycaemia (masking symptoms); cold extremities (peripheral vasoconstriction); worsening of peripheral vascular disease/intermittent claudication.
questions.explanation: Loss of beta2-mediated relaxation underlies these adverse effects.
questions.keyConcept: Beta2 blockade causes bronchospasm, masked hypoglycaemia and cold limbs.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Enumerate three therapeutic uses of clonidine.
questions.modelAnswer: Clonidine is used for diarrhea in diabetics with autonomic neuropathy, as pre-anesthetic medication, for morphine withdrawal, for menopausal hot flushes, for migraine prophylaxis, for hypertensive urgencies and for glaucoma.
questions.keyConcept: Clonidine treats hypertension, opioid withdrawal, hot flushes and migraine prophylaxis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Enumerate two hypertensive emergencies treated by labetalol.
questions.modelAnswer: Labetalol is used for hypertension during pregnancy and labor (pre-eclampsia), pheochromocytoma, clonidine rebound hypertension and the cheese (tyramine) reaction.
questions.keyConcept: Labetalol treats pre-eclampsia, pheochromocytoma and clonidine-rebound/cheese-reaction crises.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: First-dose postural hypotension with alpha-adrenoceptor blockers can be avoided. Explain how.
questions.modelAnswer: It can be minimized by giving a small dose (about 1 mg) at bedtime.
questions.keyConcept: Give a small first dose at bedtime to avoid first-dose hypotension.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Labetalol: mention the mechanism and list two therapeutic uses.
questions.modelAnswer: Mechanism: a mixed alpha1 and non-selective beta-adrenoceptor antagonist; it blocks alpha1 receptors (causing vasodilatation) and beta1/beta2 receptors (reducing heart rate and contractility). Uses: hypertensive emergencies (e.g. eclampsia); phaeochromocytoma; aortic dissection.
questions.explanation: Combined alpha and beta blockade lowers blood pressure rapidly.
questions.keyConcept: Labetalol blocks both alpha1 and beta receptors.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: List four differences between lipophilic and hydrophilic beta blockers.
questions.modelAnswer: Lipophilic blockers readily cross the BBB (more CNS effects), undergo hepatic metabolism, have a shorter half-life and more hepatic drug interactions, and suit migraine/anxiety/tremors. Hydrophilic blockers have poor CNS penetration (fewer CNS effects), renal excretion, a longer half-life and fewer interactions, and are preferred in liver disease or the elderly.
questions.explanation: Lipid solubility governs CNS entry, metabolism and half-life.
questions.keyConcept: Lipophilic vs hydrophilic blockers differ in CNS entry and clearance.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: List four possible adverse effects of long-term use of alpha methyldopa.
questions.modelAnswer: Sedation, drowsiness, depression; bradycardia; positive Coombs' test leading to haemolytic anaemia; hepatotoxicity (hepatitis); drug-induced lupus-like syndrome; Parkinsonism.
questions.explanation: Methyldopa has central, haematological and hepatic toxicities.
questions.keyConcept: Long-term methyldopa risks haemolysis, hepatitis and CNS effects.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: List four therapeutic uses of beta blockers due to beta-1 blockade.
questions.modelAnswer: Through beta-1 blockade, beta blockers are used in hypertension, ischemic heart disease, cardiac arrhythmias, systolic heart failure, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (relaxing the septum to reduce outflow resistance) and hyperthyroidism or thyrotoxic crisis (propranolol).
questions.keyConcept: Beta-1 blockade treats hypertension, ischemia, arrhythmias, heart failure and HOCM.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: List four therapeutic uses of beta blockers secondary to beta1 blockade.
questions.modelAnswer: Hypertension (decrease cardiac output and renin release); ischaemic heart disease/angina pectoris (decrease myocardial oxygen demand); hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (reduce outflow obstruction); cardiac arrhythmias (slow AV conduction, suppress ectopic beats).
questions.explanation: Beta1 blockade reduces cardiac workload and conduction.
questions.keyConcept: Beta1 blockade underlies the cardiac uses of beta-blockers.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: List the vasodilator beta blockers.
questions.modelAnswer: Carvedilol, labetalol, nebivolol.
questions.explanation: These beta-blockers also produce vasodilatation.
questions.keyConcept: Carvedilol, labetalol and nebivolol are vasodilator beta-blockers.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: List three non-cardiovascular adverse effects of beta blockers.
questions.modelAnswer: Bronchospasm; CNS effects (fatigue, depression, insomnia, nightmares); hypoglycaemia (especially in diabetics by masking warning signs); erectile dysfunction; cold extremities.
questions.explanation: Beta blockade affects lungs, brain, metabolism and sexual function.
questions.keyConcept: Beta-blockers have notable non-cardiac adverse effects.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: List two advantages of nebivolol.
questions.modelAnswer: Nebivolol does not induce significant bradycardia, does not cause sexual dysfunction and is useful in the treatment of hypertension.
questions.keyConcept: Nebivolol avoids bradycardia and sexual dysfunction while treating hypertension.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: List two adverse effects of alpha methyldopa.
questions.modelAnswer: Sedation and bradycardia (also depression, Parkinsonism, hepatitis, haemolytic anaemia, lupus).
questions.explanation: Methyldopa commonly causes central and haematological effects.
questions.keyConcept: Methyldopa causes sedation and bradycardia among other effects.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: List two adverse effects of beta blockers due to beta-2 blockade.
questions.modelAnswer: Beta-2 blockade can cause cold extremities, bronchospasm, prolongation of insulin-induced hypoglycemia, glucose intolerance and hyperkalemia in susceptible patients.
questions.keyConcept: Beta-2 blockade causes bronchospasm, cold extremities and prolonged hypoglycemia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: List two adverse effects of beta blockers due to beta2 blockade.
questions.modelAnswer: Bronchospasm; prolongation of insulin-induced hypoglycaemia.
questions.explanation: These result from loss of beta2-mediated relaxation and glucose recovery.
questions.keyConcept: Beta2 blockade causes bronchospasm and prolonged hypoglycaemia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: List two cardioselective beta blockers and mention their advantages over non-selective ones.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples: metoprolol, atenolol. Advantages: reduced risk of bronchospasm (safer in asthma/COPD); less masking of hypoglycaemia symptoms in diabetics; less peripheral vasoconstriction (fewer cold extremities).
questions.explanation: Beta1 selectivity spares beta2-mediated effects.
questions.keyConcept: Cardioselective blockers are safer in asthma and diabetes.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: List two centrally acting alpha2 agonist drugs and mention one use for each.
questions.modelAnswer: Clonidine: used for hypertension (reduces sympathetic outflow). Alpha methyldopa: used for hypertension during pregnancy.
questions.explanation: Both lower blood pressure via central alpha2 stimulation.
questions.keyConcept: Clonidine and methyldopa are central alpha2 antihypertensives.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: List two vasodilator beta blockers.
questions.modelAnswer: Carvedilol, nebivolol and labetalol are vasodilator beta blockers.
questions.keyConcept: Carvedilol, nebivolol and labetalol are vasodilating beta blockers.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: List two vasodilator beta blockers. Discuss their mechanism and one therapeutic use for each.
questions.modelAnswer: Carvedilol: non-selective beta-blockade plus alpha1 blockade causing vasodilatation; use in chronic heart failure. Labetalol: non-selective beta-blockade plus alpha1 blockade causing vasodilatation; use in hypertensive emergencies (e.g. eclampsia). Nebivolol: highly selective beta1-blockade plus endothelial nitric oxide release causing vasodilatation; use in hypertension.
questions.explanation: Vasodilator beta-blockers add alpha1 blockade or NO release.
questions.keyConcept: Vasodilator beta-blockers combine beta blockade with vasodilatation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Mention one therapeutic use of alpha methyldopa.
questions.modelAnswer: It is used as an antihypertensive, especially in pregnancy.
questions.keyConcept: Methyldopa is an antihypertensive of choice in pregnancy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Mention one use of esmolol.
questions.modelAnswer: A single injection for supraventricular tachycardia, or an IV infusion for perioperative hypertension (e.g. pending dissecting aortic aneurysm surgery).
questions.explanation: Esmolol's ultra-short action suits acute, titratable control.
questions.keyConcept: Esmolol gives rapid, short-lived beta1 blockade for acute settings.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Mention the advantages of selective beta-1 blockers over non-selective ones.
questions.modelAnswer: Selective beta-1 blockers cause less bronchospasm, less delayed recovery from hypoglycemia and less risk of Raynaud's phenomenon.
questions.keyConcept: Selective beta-1 blockers spare bronchi, hypoglycemia recovery and peripheral circulation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Mention the advantages of selective beta blockers over non-selective ones.
questions.modelAnswer: Reduced beta2 adverse effects: less bronchospasm (safer in asthma/COPD), less masking of hypoglycaemia symptoms in diabetics, less peripheral vasoconstriction (fewer cold extremities). They are generally preferred in patients with pulmonary disease or diabetes when a beta-blocker is essential.
questions.explanation: Sparing beta2 receptors reduces respiratory and metabolic harm.
questions.keyConcept: Selective beta1 blockers spare beta2-mediated adverse effects.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Mention the mechanism of action of alpha methyldopa.
questions.modelAnswer: Alpha methyldopa is a prodrug metabolized in the brain to alpha-methyl-norepinephrine, which stimulates central alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem (nucleus tractus solitarius), reducing central sympathetic outflow and lowering blood pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Methyldopa becomes alpha-methyl-NE, a central alpha-2 agonist that lowers sympathetic outflow.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Mention two types of ischemic heart disease treated by beta blockers.
questions.modelAnswer: Beta blockers are used in angina pectoris (except vasospastic angina, which they may worsen) and in myocardial infarction (prophylactically and in the acute phase to reduce infarct size and mortality).
questions.keyConcept: Beta blockers treat classic angina and myocardial infarction but not vasospastic angina.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Nebivolol: mention its mechanism of action.
questions.modelAnswer: Nebivolol is a selective beta-1 blocker that also releases nitric oxide from vascular endothelial cells, producing vasodilation.
questions.keyConcept: Nebivolol is a beta-1 blocker that releases endothelial nitric oxide.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the main use of alpha blockers?
questions.modelAnswer: Benign prostatic hyperplasia, with (prazosin) or without (tamsulosin) coexisting essential hypertension.
questions.explanation: Alpha1 blockade relaxes prostatic and vascular smooth muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha-blockers are mainly used for BPH (with or without hypertension).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the role of beta blockers in thyrotoxicosis?
questions.modelAnswer: They inhibit the peripheral conversion of T4 into active T3, are cardio-protective, and reduce anxiety and tremors.
questions.explanation: Beta-blockers control adrenergic symptoms and T4-to-T3 conversion.
questions.keyConcept: Beta-blockers relieve thyrotoxic symptoms and reduce T3 formation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match each beta-blocker to its characteristic statement.

pairs.target: Has intrinsic sympathomimetic activity; not used in angina
Long-acting hydrophilic blocker preferred in hepatic dysfunction
Has no membrane-stabilizing activity; preferred in glaucoma

questions.explanation: Pindolol has ISA; nadolol is long-acting/hydrophilic (renally excreted, safe in liver disease); timolol lacks membrane-stabilizing activity (no corneal anesthesia); nebivolol vasodilates via endothelial NO.
questions.keyConcept: Beta-blocker distinctions: ISA, hydrophilicity, MSA, NO release.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match each beta-blocker to its therapeutic use.

pairs.target: Prophylaxis of oesophageal varices and migraine, and thyrotoxicosis
Acute dissecting aortic aneurysm and pheochromocytoma

questions.explanation: Propranolol (non-selective, lipophilic) for varices/migraine prophylaxis and thyrotoxicosis; betaxolol (topical) for glaucoma; labetalol (α/β, IV) for aortic dissection and pheochromocytoma; carvedilol (vasodilating) for hypertension and heart failure.
questions.keyConcept: Indication-based selection of beta-blockers.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match each α blocker to its profile and indication.

pairs.target: Non-selective, long-acting (irreversible) α blocker for pheochromocytoma
Selective α1 blocker for benign prostatic hyperplasia
Non-selective, short-acting α blocker for α-agonist extravasation, pheochromocytoma crisis, and clonidine rebound
Combined α1/β blocker for most hypertensive crises except heart failure

questions.explanation: Phenoxybenzamine is an irreversible non-selective α blocker; prazosin is selective α1; phentolamine is reversible short-acting non-selective; labetalol blocks α1 and β.
questions.keyConcept: Selectivity, duration, and indications of α-adrenergic blockers.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match each β blocker with its use:

pairs.target: Prophylactic in oesophageal varices & migraine & in thyrotoxicosis

questions.explanation: Propranolol is used prophylactically (varices, migraine, thyrotoxicosis); betaxolol for open-angle glaucoma; labetalol for aortic dissection/pheochromocytoma; carvedilol for hypertension and chronic heart failure.
questions.keyConcept: Clinical uses of propranolol, betaxolol, labetalol and carvedilol.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match each drug to its mechanism of action and use.

pairs.target: Vasopressor activating α1 receptors, used in postural hypotension
Central α2 receptor agonist used in hypertensive pregnant patients
Peripheral vasodilator activating D1 receptors, used in hypertensive crisis
Central α2- and imidazoline-receptor agonist used in hypertensive urgency
Long-acting β2 agonist used in asthma

questions.explanation: Midodrine (α1) treats postural hypotension; methyldopa (central α2 via α-methyl-NA) is safe in pregnancy; fenoldopam (D1) is used IV in hypertensive crisis; clonidine (central α2/imidazoline) treats hypertensive urgency; salmeterol is a LABA for asthma.
questions.keyConcept: Mechanisms and uses of α1/α2/D1/β2-acting drugs.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match the following beta blockers to the suitable statement:

pairs.target: Has intrinsic sympathomimetic activity, not used in angina
Long acting hydrophilic preferred in hepatic dysfunction
Has no membrane-stabilizing activity, preferred in glaucoma

questions.explanation: Pindolol has ISA; nadolol is long-acting and hydrophilic (renal); timolol lacks MSA so is used in glaucoma; nebivolol promotes endothelial NO release.
questions.keyConcept: Distinguishing features of pindolol, nadolol, timolol and nebivolol.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match the following α-blockers to their indication:

pairs.target: Non-selective, long acting α blocker / pheochromocytoma
Selective α-1 blocker / benign prostatic hyperplasia
Non-selective, short acting α blocker / extravasation of α agonists / hypertensive crisis in pheochromocytoma / clonidine rebound
α-1/β blocker / most hypertensive crisis except heart failure

questions.explanation: Phenoxybenzamine = irreversible non-selective α-blocker for pheochromocytoma; prazosin = selective α1 for BPH/HTN; phentolamine = reversible short-acting α-blocker; labetalol = α/β blocker for hypertensive crises.
questions.keyConcept: Indications of phenoxybenzamine, prazosin, phentolamine and labetalol.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross-match the following drugs with their possible indication.
questions.explanation: Clonidine treats hypertension and hot flushes; methyldopa is first-line in pregnancy; labetalol is used in eclampsia; propranolol treats thyrotoxicosis and migraine; tamsulosin relieves BPH.
questions.keyConcept: Each adrenergic drug has a signature clinical indication.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with severe hypotension is given intravenous noradrenaline. Which of the following drugs antagonises both the vascular and cardiac actions of the drug?
questions.explanation: Carvedilol blocks both beta (cardiac) and alpha1 (vascular) receptors, antagonising both actions of noradrenaline.
questions.keyConcept: Carvedilol blocks both alpha and beta actions of noradrenaline.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with severe hypotension is given Nor-epinephrine. Which of the following drugs antagonizes both the vascular and cardiac actions of the drug?
questions.explanation: Carvedilol blocks both α (vascular) and β (cardiac) receptors, so it antagonizes both actions of norepinephrine; the others are β-selective only.
questions.keyConcept: Carvedilol (α+β blocker) antagonizes both vascular and cardiac effects.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with severe hypotension is given norepinephrine. Which of the following drugs antagonizes both its vascular and cardiac actions?
questions.explanation: Carvedilol blocks both α (vascular) and β (cardiac) receptors, antagonizing both actions of norepinephrine.
questions.keyConcept: Carvedilol (α+β blocker) opposes both vascular and cardiac NE effects.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with severe hypotension is given norepinephrine. Which of the following drugs antagonizes both the vascular and cardiac actions of the drug?
questions.explanation: Carvedilol blocks both alpha (vascular) and beta (cardiac) receptors, antagonizing both actions of norepinephrine; the others block only beta-1.
questions.keyConcept: Carvedilol blocks both alpha and beta actions.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Adverse reactions of beta blockers do not include:
questions.explanation: Beta-blockers do not block alpha receptors, so postural hypotension is not a typical adverse effect; the others are recognized.
questions.keyConcept: Postural hypotension is not a typical beta-blocker effect.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All of the following regarding adrenaline are true except:
options: Should be avoided with beta blockers, thyrotoxicosis or ischemic heart disease
Relaxation of the GIT wall by stimulation of alpha and beta receptors
No change in mean BP at therapeutic doses
questions.explanation: Adrenaline alters blood pressure (raising systolic via beta-1/alpha and lowering diastolic via beta-2), so claiming no change is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Adrenaline changes blood pressure at therapeutic doses.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: An alpha-1 receptor agonist is not effective in the treatment of:
questions.explanation: An alpha-1 agonist raises blood pressure and produces reflex bradycardia useful in supraventricular (not ventricular) tachycardia, so it is ineffective in VT.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha-1 agonists help SVT, not ventricular tachycardia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Atenolol is characterized by all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Atenolol is hydrophilic, β1-selective with renal elimination, long half-life and few CNS effects; being β1-selective it carries LESS Raynaud's risk, so D is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Atenolol: hydrophilic, renally cleared, β1-selective with less Raynaud's risk.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Beta adrenoceptor blockers have the following characters except:
options: Some block sodium channels like propranolol
They may reduce hepatic blood flow, decreasing drug metabolism
Some have an agonistic effect besides their antagonistic effect
questions.explanation: Beta-blockers decrease myocardial oxygen consumption by lowering heart rate and contractility, so increasing it is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Beta-blockers decrease myocardial oxygen demand.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Beta adrenoceptor blockers have the following characters except:
options: Some block sodium channels like propranolol
They may reduce hepatic blood flow leading to decreased metabolism
Some have agonistic effect beside their antagonistic effect
questions.explanation: Beta-blockers decrease myocardial oxygen consumption, which is the basis of their anti-anginal action, so this is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Beta-blockers reduce, not increase, myocardial oxygen consumption.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Beta blocker is useful in treatment of open angle glaucoma and essential tremors due to:
questions.explanation: β2 blockade reduces aqueous humor production (lowering intraocular pressure) and suppresses peripheral β2-mediated essential tremor.
questions.keyConcept: β2 blockade underlies both glaucoma and essential-tremor benefit.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Beta blockers are useful in the treatment of open angle glaucoma and essential tremors due to:
questions.explanation: Beta-2 blockade reduces aqueous humor formation (glaucoma) and dampens beta-2-mediated essential tremor.
questions.keyConcept: Beta-2 blockade underlies both effects.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Beta blockers may be used in the treatment of all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Beta-blockers slow AV conduction and are contraindicated in AV block, which they would worsen.
questions.keyConcept: Beta-blockers are contraindicated in AV block.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cardio-selective Beta blockers include:
questions.explanation: Metoprolol, atenolol and bisoprolol are β1-selective, so both pairs A and D are cardioselective.
questions.keyConcept: Metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol are cardioselective (β1) blockers.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: CNS therapeutic uses of propranolol include:
questions.explanation: Per the source key the answer is social anxiety disorders. Note: propranolol is also used for essential tremor, so option D (A+B) is arguably more complete — flag for review; sexual dysfunction is a side effect, not a use.
questions.keyConcept: Propranolol treats performance/social anxiety (and essential tremor) (item flagged).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross-match the following to its hemodynamic effect - Dobutamine:
options: Renal vasodilator, positive inotrope and chronotrope with vasopressor effects at high dose
Weak positive inotrope; powerful splanchnic vasodilator
Positive inotrope with minimal effect on blood pressure or heart rate
Increases blood pressure with reflex vagal bradycardia
questions.explanation: Dobutamine is a beta-1 agonist that increases contractility with little net effect on blood pressure or heart rate.
questions.keyConcept: Dobutamine is a relatively pure positive inotrope.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross-match the following to its hemodynamic effect - Dopamine:
options: Renal vasodilator, positive inotrope and chronotrope with vasopressor effects at high dose
Weak positive inotrope; powerful splanchnic vasodilator
Positive inotrope with minimal effect on blood pressure or heart rate
Increases blood pressure with reflex vagal bradycardia
questions.explanation: Dopamine produces dose-dependent renal vasodilation (D1), inotropy/chronotropy (beta-1) and, at high doses, alpha-mediated vasopressor effects.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine has dose-dependent renal, cardiac and pressor effects.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross-match the following to its hemodynamic effect - Dopexamine:
options: Renal vasodilator, positive inotrope and chronotrope with vasopressor effects at high dose
Weak positive inotrope; powerful splanchnic vasodilator
Positive inotrope with minimal effect on blood pressure or heart rate
Increases blood pressure with reflex vagal bradycardia
questions.explanation: Dopexamine is a weak positive inotrope (beta-2) and a powerful splanchnic/renal vasodilator via dopamine receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Dopexamine is a weak inotrope and splanchnic vasodilator.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross-match the following to its hemodynamic effect - Phenylephrine:
options: Renal vasodilator, positive inotrope and chronotrope with vasopressor effects at high dose
Weak positive inotrope; powerful splanchnic vasodilator
Positive inotrope with minimal effect on blood pressure or heart rate
Increases blood pressure with reflex vagal bradycardia
questions.explanation: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha-1 agonist that raises blood pressure and triggers reflex vagal bradycardia.
questions.keyConcept: Phenylephrine raises BP with reflex bradycardia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Dopamine is preferred to dobutamine in cardiogenic shock with hypotension or renal impairment because:
options: The D1 effect of dopamine induces renal vasodilation and increases renal blood flow
Dopamine induces an alpha-mediated vasopressor effect
The beta-1 selective effect of dobutamine increases arrhythmia risk compared to dopamine
questions.explanation: Dopamine both improves renal perfusion via D1 receptors and supports blood pressure via alpha-mediated vasoconstriction, making it preferable when hypotension and renal impairment coexist.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine gives renal D1 vasodilation plus alpha vasopressor support.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Epinephrine-induced hypokalemia is due to:
questions.explanation: Epinephrine lowers serum potassium by promoting cellular (including hepatic) uptake of K+ and through renin-related effects, so both A and B apply.
questions.keyConcept: Epinephrine drives K+ into cells, lowering serum K+.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Esmolol has an ultra-short duration of action due to:
questions.explanation: Esmolol contains an ester linkage rapidly cleaved by red-cell and plasma esterases, giving a half-life of about 9 minutes.
questions.keyConcept: Esmolol is rapidly inactivated by plasma esterases (t½ ≈ 9 min).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Esmolol is used in:
questions.explanation: Esmolol is an ultra-short-acting cardioselective β-blocker given IV for perioperative hypertension and acute supraventricular arrhythmias. It is not used for chronic heart failure (oral agents like carvedilol/bisoprolol are).
questions.keyConcept: Esmolol: ultra-short-acting IV β1-blocker for acute perioperative hypertension and SVT.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Esmolol is used in:
questions.explanation: Esmolol, an ultra-short-acting beta-1 blocker, is used for perioperative hypertension and acute supraventricular arrhythmias.
questions.keyConcept: Esmolol treats perioperative HTN and SVT.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Hydrophilic beta-blockers have a long duration of action, EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Esmolol has an ultra-short duration because it is rapidly hydrolyzed by plasma esterases, despite limited lipid solubility. Atenolol and nadolol are hydrophilic and long-acting (renally excreted).
questions.keyConcept: Esmolol is brief because of plasma esterase hydrolysis, not its solubility.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Hydrophilic ultrashort beta adrenoceptor blocker is:
questions.explanation: Esmolol is a hydrophilic, ultra-short-acting beta1-selective blocker used intravenously.
questions.keyConcept: Esmolol is the ultra-short-acting IV beta1 blocker.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: In oesophageal varices, the beta2-blocking effect of non-selective blockers reduces portal blood flow secondary to:
questions.explanation: Beta2 blockade leaves alpha-mediated splanchnic vasoconstriction unopposed, reducing portal blood flow.
questions.keyConcept: Non-selective blockers lower portal flow via unopposed splanchnic vasoconstriction.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: In prophylaxis of oesophageal varices, the β2 blocking effect(s) of non-selective β blockers reduce(s) portal blood flow 2° to:
questions.explanation: β2 blockade leaves α-mediated splanchnic vasoconstriction unopposed, reducing portal inflow; reduced cardiac output is the β1 contribution.
questions.keyConcept: β2 blockade → unopposed splanchnic vasoconstriction → lower portal flow.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Labetalol is not:
options: Selective alpha1 and non-selective beta blocker
questions.explanation: Labetalol is used for hypertensive emergencies but is not typically used for heart failure (carvedilol is preferred).
questions.keyConcept: Labetalol is not a standard heart-failure beta-blocker.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Lipophilic beta blockers have a short duration of action Except:
questions.explanation: Atenolol is hydrophilic (renally eliminated) with a longer duration, so it is the exception among these lipophilic, short-acting agents.
questions.keyConcept: Atenolol is hydrophilic and longer-acting, unlike lipophilic β-blockers.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Metabolic actions of epinephrine include all of the following except:
options: Lipolysis by beta-2 and beta-3 stimulation
Decreases serum K+ by beta-2 stimulation
Inhibition of insulin secretion by beta-2
questions.explanation: Epinephrine inhibits insulin secretion through alpha-2 receptors, not beta-2, so this statement is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Insulin secretion is inhibited via alpha-2 receptors.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Metoprolol is characterized by all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Metoprolol is lipophilic and extensively hepatically metabolized, so it is NOT suitable in hepatic impairment.
questions.keyConcept: Hepatically metabolized metoprolol is unsuitable in liver impairment.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Non-selective βB with vasodilator effect 2° to α blockade:
questions.explanation: Both labetalol and carvedilol are non-selective β-blockers with additional α-blocking (vasodilator) activity.
questions.keyConcept: Labetalol and carvedilol combine β- and α-blockade.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Non-selective βB with vasodilator effect 2° to α blockade:
questions.explanation: Labetalol and carvedilol are non-selective β-blockers with additional α-blocking vasodilatation (nebivolol vasodilates via NO, not α-blockade).
questions.keyConcept: Labetalol and carvedilol vasodilate via α-blockade.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Non-selective beta-blocker with vasodilator effect secondary to alpha blockade:
